name: Hydrolyzed whey protein

lead: Hydrolyzed whey protein is whey that has been partially pre-digested, so its protein is already split into shorter peptide chains. People use it as a protein powder to help meet protein targets while training, which supports muscle growth and the fuller physique that goes with it.

Hydrolysates typically cost more than whey concentrate or isolate, and the smaller peptides may be less allergenic, which is why they appear in hypoallergenic infant formulas. Research on whey generally shows benefits for muscle mass alongside resistance training; direct comparisons of hydrolysate with other forms are fewer.

paras: It is taken as a powder mixed into a shake, commonly around training, as one protein source among others. Some people choose it over concentrate or isolate because they expect faster digestion.

Whey proteins can cause reactions in people with milk allergy. Hydrolysate products can taste more bitter and cost more than other whey forms, and people with kidney or other medical conditions are usually advised to check protein intake with a clinician.

chain: Support recovery and muscle protein synthesis after training
More muscle over time with continued lifting
angle.text: Hydrolyzed whey is a convenient protein source for people building muscle through resistance training. Protein supports the recovery and muscle growth that lead to a fuller, more muscular physique.

lead: Hydrolyzed whey protein (whey hydrolysate, WPH) is whey that has been predigested, or partially hydrolysed, so that its protein is broken into smaller peptides for easier metabolism.[1] It is a variant of whey protein, the milk-derived supplement widely used by people who lift weights.

For appearance, the route is a chain: protein intake supports recovery and muscle protein synthesis after resistance training, which over time supports more muscle mass and a more developed physique.[1][2] Whey is mainly used for muscle growth, and a 2010 EFSA review found it about as effective as other protein sources for strength and lean mass, findings that apply to whey generally rather than hydrolysates specifically.[1]

Compared with concentrate (29 to 89 percent protein by weight, retaining some fat and lactose) and isolate (over 90 percent), hydrolysate is described as the fastest-digesting form, and it typically costs more.[1][3] Its smaller peptide chains are also the reason it appears in hypoallergenic infant formulas and medical foods.[4][5]

Research on the form itself is narrower than research on whey as a whole: a 2009 study in young men compared whey hydrolysate with casein and soy for muscle protein synthesis, while most trials on muscle mass and strength use whey generally.[6][2]
infobox: Smaller peptides; fastest digestion rate; typically higher cost; can taste bitter[4][3]

paras: Whey is the liquid left over when milk is coagulated in cheese production, and its main protein components are alpha-lactalbumin, beta-lactoglobulin, serum albumin and immunoglobulins.[1] Four commercial forms exist: concentrate, isolate (over 90 percent protein), hydrolysate (predigested and typically costlier) and native whey extracted from skim milk.[1]

Hydrolysis uses enzymes or acid to split protein into shorter peptide chains before the product is dried. Enzymatic hydrolysis such as with pancreatic protease stops at the peptide level and imitates natural digestion, whereas prolonged acid hydrolysis reduces protein to individual amino acids.[4] Whey protein is generally described as more bioavailable than casein or soy, and hydrolysates are positioned as the pre-digested end of the whey range.[1][3]

In sport and bodybuilding, whey is taken mainly to support muscle growth, with post-exercise intake raising free amino acids that support recovery and protein synthesis.[1] Wikipedia notes that protein powder is the most popular bodybuilding supplement form and that users cite convenience, cost compared with meat and fish, and ease of preparation as reasons; powders are usually mixed with water, milk or juice and taken around training or in place of a meal.[3]

Whey is high in essential and branched-chain amino acids and has the highest cysteine content of the common proteins, and hydrolysate is described as having the fastest digestion rate among whey forms.[3] People who choose hydrolysate over concentrate or isolate commonly do so for this expected speed, or for lower lactose and fat, though most evidence on muscle outcomes is for whey generally.[3][2]

Total intake matters in the research. A 2018 meta-analysis by Morton and colleagues, summarised on Wikipedia, found muscle growth rose with protein intake up to roughly 1.6 g per kg of body weight per day with little added benefit beyond that, and a 2020 analysis by Tagawa and colleagues found benefits plateau once basic requirements are met in resistance-trained people.[3]

In infant nutrition, partially and extensively hydrolysed whey are used in formulas for infants who need or may benefit from lower-allergen options.[7][8] A 2013 American Academy of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology committee review stated that for high-risk infants who cannot be exclusively breast-fed, hydrolyzed formula appears to offer advantages in preventing allergic disease and cow's milk allergy.[5] Wikipedia reports that the US FDA approved a label for partially hydrolyzed proteins in 2017 while a meta-analysis found insufficient evidence for that use.[4]

In clinical nutrition, a 2020 review of enteral formulas for critically ill patients noted that hydrolyzed whey protein reaches the highest amino acid plasma levels when given in large doses, and a 2021 meta-analysis examined whey or casein hydrolysate in fortifiers for very low birth weight infants.[9][10]

Partial hydrolysis exposes hydrophobic side chains, which can make peptides taste bitter; Wikipedia gives the example of soy protein, where bitterness peaks at a mean peptide size of about 2 to 4 kDa and falls with further hydrolysis.[4] Hydrolysed protein also has higher osmolarity than intact protein, which may cause diarrhoea in infants, although this is not seen in adults and dogs.[4] Hydrolysates typically cost more than concentrate or isolate.[1]

Whey proteins are among the milk proteins that can cause milk allergy, although casein is the major milk allergen.[1] Wikipedia states that an allergen needs at least two IgE-binding epitopes to trigger a reaction and that incomplete hydrolysis can leave those intact, so hydrolysates are not automatically allergen-free.[4]

In the United States, supplement manufacturers are not required to give the FDA evidence of safety before marketing under the 1994 Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act.[3] Wikipedia reports that a 2015 Consumer Reports test found arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury in several protein powders and that a 2015 CBC investigation found 'protein spiking' with amino-acid filler was not uncommon, findings many companies disputed.[3] People with kidney or other medical conditions are usually advised to review protein intake with a clinician.

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of seven randomised trials (591 participants) in older people with sarcopenia included supplements based on concentrated, isolated or hydrolysed whey during resistance training. It reported a small pooled effect favouring whey plus training for appendicular muscle mass (standardised mean difference 0.24) and a handgrip-strength difference of about 2.3 kg with high heterogeneity; the authors described the effect sizes as small and rated the evidence quality as low to very low.[2]

A 2009 study by Tang and colleagues in 18 healthy young men gave each participant a shake with 10 g of essential amino acids from whey hydrolysate, micellar casein or soy after a one-legged resistance workout. Whey produced the largest rise in blood amino acids; both whey and soy raised muscle protein synthesis more than casein at rest and after exercise, and after exercise whey exceeded soy. The authors suggested digestion speed and leucine content as explanations.[6]
Infant-formula trials have assessed extensively and partially hydrolysed whey for growth and safety against standard formulas.[7][8]

lore.intro: Hydrolyzed whey is discussed in sports-nutrition circles as the fastest and most easily absorbed whey, usually weighed against its higher price and bitter taste.[3][4]
